item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
item.description:
Source: www.anthropic.com

Top Comment:

> As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

As impressive as this sounds, whether it is tech teams or agent farms, the progress slows down considerably as the codebase grows. The real pain was seldom about shipping v1, but was more about how the v8 scales and how easy it is to get there, how robust the system remains between versions, and how constraints are held.

A huge part of the challenge is to pick/choose the design and implementation strategy that can only come from experience. That is one of the primary reasons why it's an absurd advice to me to let the llm do the goalseek and freestyle. This may be a no big deal on microservice or any managed runtime software that is an update away, but on an embedded or a high availability system where the field upgrade and hardware replacement costs could bankrupt a business.

if llm designed a circuit, will you bankroll it?

TBH, if you are launching a startup, it might not be a terrible idea to incorporate in Canada. Canada has the notion of federal incorporation in addition to each province having its own corporate registry. Federal corporations can exist in any province but all the filings are done in one place.

And there is a refundable tax credit for R&D that works out to about 60% of engineers' salaries (in most provinces). item.title: Show HN: Every satellite that passed over any place this week, and its photos
item.description:
Source: www.watched.earth

hey HN, i built this because I'm a satellite nerd who was bored this past weekend.

type in any place and it finds every satellite that passed over it in the last 7 days (SGP4 on the CelesTrak catalog, tracking 17k+ objects and runs in your browser in about half a second), then pulls the real Sentinel-2 / Landsat / NASA images from those passes.

fun fact: all ~17k objects in orbit are drawn on the GPU, solving Kepler's equation every frame. also cool is that Sentinel-2 timestamps are often 5-10 min off from when the sat actually crosses your spot, so some cool math was involved in making it accurate on the site.

it only shows real images taken from those exact satellites, and it never store your location.

code: https://github.com/dev-Armaan/satellites

would love feedback, contributions, or whatever else you guys can offer!

Top Comment:

Beautifully done, at so many levels: the pincushion view of just how much stuff is up there; the rendering of the orbit of each satellite; the ground track of its aperture; the time series of its passes. So many data sources seamlessly integrated. Even if Claude wrote every line of code, knowing what to ask for is quite a feat.

Amazing.

Something seems wrong here. They took a non-trivial piece of human-written code that has had bugs in the past, formally verified the whole library, and found zero bugs?

I can believe that it's possible to get the LLM to write proofs, but I can't believe there were zero bugs in the system they verified. I wonder if they got the theorems wrong, or if they only proved narrow properties of the system.

I've had Claude formally verify crypto and data storage formats. It wrote theorems that looked fine and the formal verification passed but the resulting code contained many, many bugs that other implementations of the same things found with ad hoc testing.

The way the announcement is written, we should expect zero bugs in libsignal moving forward, and I guess time will tell whether that happens or not.

item.description:
Source: www.anthropocenemagazine.org

https://www.cell.com/cell-reports-physical-science/fulltext/...

Top Comment:

Specialty cut flower grower here. Backyard scale, but we're profitable and have received some grants so that means we have had a USDA relationship for a couple years. The rep I've talked to and am closest with is skeptical of agrivoltaics due to past dealings with solar companies (not sure what she means). There doesn't seem to be enough reliable public data to make it seem like the win-win-win we want it to be. In their mind, you're adding a non-ag industry to the land and that could have downstream consequences in a generation. Maybe you're scheming to get the land re-zoned for light industrial; I honestly have no idea what they're thinking, but they're averse toward it.

Most flowers in 7b don't want extreme sun. We use shade cloth frequently, so solar coverage would be fine and of course have the energy co-production. Cut flowers aren't harvested mechanically at our scale, so we wouldn't have to worry about tractor access.

Meanwhile, more and more food is produced under cover for a lot of good reasons. Polytunnels, glass houses. You might get some summer shade from solar but what about season extension at the beginning of spring/end of fall? Depending on your crop and location, that could mean 4-8 extra weeks a year. What if you do geothermal energy generation for the tunnel? Now you can grow through the winter and not need the same footprint as solar. That's more appealing to me.

Anyway, I'm forever mad at corn ethanol and we should at least replace all that with solar farms. That's probably the right place to start. But also, again, zoning...

item.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
item.description:
Source: simonwillison.net

Top Comment:

Around '05 or so, the house we were staying in started beeping. Smoke alarm sounds, as usual. For almost a day we couldn't find the source. Contacted the owners -- they didn't know it either. They bought the house few years prior, so not much of a help.

Standing in the hallways listening at different angles, as the article says, didn't help. No Fable in '05 either.

So I had to improvise. Got a ~1 meter stick and two headphones (every headphone is a microphone, even if it sucks as a microphone). Plugged them into the stereo mic port, and started recording in Audacity. The phase shift between L and R pointed directly to the source. Took about 4 or 5 beeps to get the sucker.

Turns out, it was hiding above the ceiling tiles in the garage. My wife still tells this story to all her friends as one of my biggest life achievements. Everything I shipped, the companies I founded -- pales in comparison to finding a dead smoke alarm

item.title: A primer on GPUs and kernel optimization
item.description:

Top Comment:

Crazy to not see a word about benchmarking/evaluation of the kernels.

IMO at this time when all performant GPU kernels are generated/hill-climbed, its the largest source of error we see.

Should be kernel run with a hot or cold cache in practice? Should your kernel be bitwise equivalent to a ref? What error margins should your kernel have to ref? How many times are you running the kernel to avoid thermal noise? Are you running on separate GPUs to avoid overfitting the current hardware? Can you cudagraph-compiling your kernel to remove launch overhead? Are you A/B B/A interleaving your kernel/reference runs to avoid running thermal bias?
